reigns.tagline: The fake friar who knocked on Monaco's door
reigns.previously: Genoa's civil war has thrown the Guelph Grimaldis out of the city.
paragraphs: Genoa in the 1290s was a city at war with itself. The Guelphs backed the pope, the Ghibellines backed the emperor, and the Ghibellines were on top. The Grimaldis, proud Guelphs, were driven out. West along the coast stood a Genoese fortress on the Rock of Monaco, with a sheltered harbour below. François Grimaldi, nicknamed Malizia, roughly “the Crafty”, had his eye on it.

On the night of 8 January 1297, so the story goes, a friar in a Franciscan habit knocked at the gate and asked for shelter. The guards let him in. Out came a sword from under the robe, and his men stormed in behind him. The fortress was theirs. His cousin Rainier was in on the plot. Two monks waving swords still hold up the Grimaldi coat of arms today.

Holding the Rock was harder than taking it. Genoa wanted its fortress back, and in 1301 it got it. Malizia never ruled Monaco again and died in 1309. Rainier did better, becoming an admiral for the King of France. But the family had tasted Monaco, and they would keep coming back.

claims.text: François got into the fortress disguised as a Franciscan friar.
claims.note: The seizure of 1297 is well recorded. The friar disguise is the family's founding story and comes from later retellings.

claims.text: The Grimaldi coat of arms is held up by two monks with swords.
claims.note: You can see them on Monaco's state arms today. They are usually read as a nod to the 1297 raid.

claims.text: Genoa took the Rock back in 1301.
claims.note: Standard in every history of Monaco; the Grimaldis only regained it 30 years later.

reigns.hook: Monaco belongs to Genoa again. But Rainier has a son, Charles, and Charles wants the Rock back.

reigns.tagline: The Rock back in Genoese hands
reigns.previously: The Grimaldis lose Monaco four years after taking it.
paragraphs: After François Grimaldi's famous capture of the Rock in 1297, the Grimaldis were driven out in 1301. Monaco went back to Genoa, which was itself torn between rival Guelph and Ghibelline factions.
Records of who actually held the fortress in these thirty years are thin. The Grimaldis, Guelph exiles from Genoa, kept fighting to return, and in 1331 Charles Grimaldi finally did.
reigns.hook: Charles Grimaldi retakes Monaco and builds it into a real lordship.

reigns.tagline: The Grimaldi who came back and went shopping
reigns.reignEnded: Died as Genoa took it back
reigns.previously: Genoa has the Rock back. Malizia dies in 1309 without regaining it.
paragraphs: Thirty years after Malizia lost the Rock, his cousin Rainier's son Charles got it back. Genoa was busy tearing itself apart again, and on 12 September 1331 the Grimaldis were back behind the walls. This time Charles wanted more than a fortress. He wanted a little state.

So he went shopping. He bought Menton along the coast in 1346 and Roquebrune in 1355. He paid for it as a soldier for hire, fighting for the King of France in the Hundred Years' War. At Crécy in 1346 he helped lead the Genoese crossbowmen, who were shot to pieces by the English longbows. From 1352 he shared the lordship with his uncle Antoine and his sons Rainier and Gabriel.
Genoa never forgave the loss. In 1357 a Genoese force laid siege to the Rock. Charles died that year, as the walls were about to fall, and his heirs were left to make a deal.

claims.text: Charles helped lead the Genoese crossbowmen at Crécy in 1346.
claims.note: Later histories name a Carlo Grimaldi and an Ottone Doria as the crossbowmen's captains. That this Grimaldi was Monaco's Charles is the usual reading, not a certainty.

claims.text: Charles bought Menton in 1346 and Roquebrune in 1355.
claims.note: Both towns came to him in those years and appear in all the standard histories; Roquebrune is sometimes said to have been taken rather than bought.

reigns.hook: Genoa's soldiers are at the gates, and Charles is dead. His heirs still hold the Rock, but for how long, and at what price?

reigns.title: Genoa Takes the Rock
reigns.tagline: The Grimaldis sell up and wait it out in Menton
reigns.previously: Charles I dies as Genoa besieges the Rock and takes it back.
paragraphs: In 1357 the Genoese came for their fortress. Charles I was dead, and his heirs had no hope of holding out. So the family sold up. For 20,000 florins, in the name of his son Rainier II, they handed the Rock to the besiegers and walked away. Genoa was back in charge, under Doge Simone Boccanegra.

The Grimaldis did not vanish. They kept Menton and Roquebrune down the coast, and Rainier made a living as a soldier for France and Naples. For almost 40 years the family looked out at the Rock they no longer owned.

Genoa had its own troubles. Doges came and went, Adornos and Fregosos and Guarcos, in a blur of coups. By the 1390s the city was in such a mess that it would soon hand itself over to the King of France.

claims.text: Rainier II gave up the Rock to Genoa for 20,000 florins.
claims.note: The deal and the sum are in the standard histories. Rainier is usually said to be born in 1350, which would make him a child who signed nothing himself.

claims.text: Simone Boccanegra, the doge who took the Rock, was poisoned in 1363.
claims.note: He died suddenly after a banquet and Genoese chroniclers spoke of poison. Nothing was proven.

reigns.hook: Genoa is falling apart, and Monaco's garrison is far from home. In January 1395 Charles I's son Louis sees his chance.

reigns.tagline: Grabbed the Rock twice, gave it up twice
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the Rock in a raid
reigns.reignEnded: Handed the Rock back to Genoa
reigns.previously: Genoa holds the Rock. The Grimaldis keep only Menton and Roquebrune.
paragraphs: For almost 40 years the Grimaldis had watched their Rock from Menton. In January 1395 Charles I's son Louis decided to stop watching. He took the fortress, and his young nephew Jean, Rainier II's boy, was named lord alongside him. Genoa was in chaos and briefly could not stop him.

It did not last. By 19 December 1395 the Genoese had the Rock back. Louis waited, and on 11 May 1397 he took it again, this time for five years. But Genoa was now under the King of France, and the pressure only grew. On 5 November 1402 Louis gave up the Rock. He died the same year.

claims.text: Louis seized Monaco twice, in 1395 and again in 1397.
claims.note: Both seizures and the 1402 surrender are in the Genoese chronicle of Giorgio Stella and the standard Monaco histories.

reigns.hook: Genoa holds the Rock again, and this time it keeps it for 17 years. Louis's nephew Jean is still out there, and he has two brothers and money.

reigns.tagline: Seventeen years without the Grimaldis
reigns.reignEnded: The three Grimaldi brothers retook it
reigns.previously: Louis Grimaldi loses Monaco to Genoa again.
paragraphs: In 1402 Louis Grimaldi had to give Monaco back to Genoa, which was then ruled by the French and later by Montferrat. The fortress was held for Genoa through years of upheaval there.
In 1419 Louis's nephews, the brothers Jean, Ambroise and Antoine Grimaldi, retook the Rock. This time the family kept it.
reigns.hook: Jean Grimaldi and his brothers hold Monaco for good.

reigns.tagline: The lord who bought his family home back
reigns.previously: Louis gives the Rock back to Genoa. It stays Genoese for 17 years.
paragraphs: Jean was Rainier II's son, named co-lord with his uncle Louis as a boy in 1395. In June 1419 he and his brothers Ambroise and Antoine got the Rock back, this time mostly with money.

At first the three brothers ran it together. Then they split the family lands: Jean kept Monaco, and his brothers took Menton and Roquebrune. Jean married Pomellina Fregoso, from one of Genoa's top political families, and held on for 35 years through all the wars of the region. That long grip is why the 1419 recovery counts as the one that stuck.
His will made a key choice for the future. It let the lordship pass to daughters if there was no son. Jean died on 8 May 1454 and his son Catalan took over.

claims.text: From 1419 the Grimaldis held Monaco for good.
claims.note: Monaco's own histories date the lasting recovery to 1419. Apart from the French Revolution, the family has held it ever since.

claims.text: Jean's will allowed the lordship to pass through women.
claims.note: The family histories say Jean allowed a woman to inherit if her husband took the Grimaldi name and arms; that rule was the basis of Claudine's claim three years later.

reigns.hook: Jean's son Catalan takes over. He has a little girl, no sons, and not much time.

reigns.tagline: Three years, one daughter, one clever will
reigns.previously: Jean I dies after 35 years. His will lets daughters inherit.
paragraphs: Catalan had only three years at the top, and his reign is mostly remembered for how it ended. He had no son. What he did have was a small daughter, Claudine, and his father's will, which allowed a girl to inherit.

So Catalan wrote his own will with a catch. Claudine would get Monaco, but she had to marry a Grimaldi cousin, so the lordship stayed in the family name. The cousin chosen was Lamberto of the Antibes branch. Catalan died in July 1457 with the plan barely in place.

claims.text: Catalan's will made Claudine heir on condition she marry a Grimaldi.
claims.note: The will's terms, including Pomellina's regency, are given in the standard histories of Monaco.

reigns.hook: Monaco's new ruler is a girl of about six. Her grandmother is in charge, and a cousin from Antibes is waiting for his bride.

reigns.tagline: A six-year-old lady and a fight over her
reigns.previously: Catalan dies with no son. Monaco goes to his small daughter Claudine.
paragraphs: Claudine was about six when she became Lady of Monaco. She is the only woman to rule it in this whole era. In practice her grandmother Pomellina Fregoso ran things, and Pomellina had ideas of her own about who should be in charge.

The family deal said otherwise. Claudine's cousin Lamberto Grimaldi of Antibes was supposed to marry her and take the reins. In March 1458 he took over. The wedding waited until 1465, when Claudine was old enough. She lived to see one of her sons murder another, and died in 1515.

claims.text: Claudine was the only woman to rule Monaco in the Middle Ages.
claims.note: No other woman held the lordship before Louise-Hippolyte reigned in 1731; the standard lists show this.

claims.text: Pomellina Fregoso tried to keep power for herself.
claims.note: The histories describe a feud between Pomellina's party and Lamberto. How far she meant to hold on is read differently.

reigns.hook: Lamberto has the Rock. Now he has to beat Pomellina's party and win over the people of Monaco.

reigns.tagline: The cousin who married the heiress
reigns.cameToPower: Family deal and a feud won
reigns.previously: Little Claudine's power passes to her cousin Lamberto.
paragraphs: Lamberto came from the Grimaldis of Antibes, and his brothers backed him all the way. First he had to beat Pomellina Fregoso's faction, which did not want him. He won, and the people of Monaco swore him an oath of loyalty.

In 1465 he married Claudine, as her father's will required. He then ruled for over 30 years, a long run by Monaco's standards. The couple had several children, and the succession was settled on them. Lamberto died in March 1494, and their eldest son Jean took over.

claims.text: The people of Monaco swore an oath of loyalty to Lamberto.
claims.note: Recorded in the standard histories of Monaco by Saige and Labande.

reigns.hook: Jean II is lord now. His younger brother Lucien is ambitious, and he is not a patient man.

reigns.tagline: Killed by his own little brother
reigns.previously: Lamberto dies after 36 years. His eldest son Jean takes Monaco.
paragraphs: Jean II was the eldest son of Lamberto and Claudine. He came to power in his mid-twenties and held it for ten years. Not much of his rule stands out. What happened at the end of it does.

On 11 October 1505 his younger brother Lucien killed him. The accounts do not agree on how or why. It may have been a quarrel that got out of hand, or a plan. Either way, Lucien walked away from his brother's body as lord of Monaco.

claims.text: Jean II was killed by his brother Lucien in 1505.
claims.note: The killing is in every account of the family and was never denied.

claims.text: The killing came out of a sudden quarrel.
claims.note: Lucien wrote that it began as a row over Jean's plan to sell Monaco and that Jean struck first; his account is self-serving, and later versions differ.

reigns.hook: Jean II is dead, and his killer is the new lord. Lucien now has to hold Monaco against Genoa, and against his own relatives.

reigns.tagline: Killed a brother, beat Genoa, killed by a nephew
reigns.previously: Jean II is dead, killed by his own younger brother Lucien.
paragraphs: Lucien got Monaco by killing his brother. He kept it by fighting. In December 1506 a Genoese army laid siege to the Rock. Lucien held out through the winter, and in March 1507 the besiegers gave up and left. It made his name.

Then came the family feud. Lucien's sister had married into the Dorias, Genoa's great sea-going clan, and the two sides fell out badly. In August 1523 his nephew Bartolomeo Doria came to Monaco on a friendly visit. On 22 August he and his men killed Lucien in the palace. Lucien's son Honoré was only a baby.

claims.text: Andrea Doria, the great admiral and Bartolomeo's relative, was in on the plot.
claims.note: His galleys were off Monaco that day, so people suspected he knew. It was never proven.

claims.text: Lucien drove off the Genoese siege in March 1507.
claims.note: The siege of 1506 to 1507 is well recorded in Genoese and French sources and the Monaco histories.

reigns.hook: Lucien lies dead in his palace, and his heir is a baby. Someone has to hold Monaco, and they will need a powerful friend.

reigns.tagline: The baby lord who put Monaco under Spain
reigns.previously: Lucien is murdered in his own palace by his nephew.
paragraphs: Honoré was nine months old when his father was killed. His uncle Agostino Grimaldi, Bishop of Grasse, ran Monaco for him. Agostino wanted protection from the Dorias and from Genoa, and he found it. In 1524 treaties signed at Burgos and Tordesillas put Monaco under the protection of the Emperor Charles V and Spain.

Other relatives kept governing for Honoré until 1540. Then he ruled for himself for 40 more years. Spain's friendship came with strings, and Monaco slowly turned into a Spanish outpost on the French coast. Honoré married his cousin Isabella Grimaldi, and they had sons.
He died on 7 October 1581 after a reign of 58 years, one of the longest in Monaco's history. His son Charles took over.

claims.text: The 1524 treaties put Monaco under Spanish protection.
claims.note: The treaties of Burgos and Tordesillas are well documented and cited in all the standard histories.

claims.text: Agostino Grimaldi ran Monaco for the baby Honoré.
claims.note: The bishop's regency, until his death in 1532, appears in Saige and Labande.

reigns.hook: Honoré I is dead after 58 years. His son Charles inherits Monaco and its Spanish protectors.

reigns.tagline: Eight quiet years in Spain's shadow
reigns.previously: Honoré I dies after almost 60 years as lord of Monaco.
paragraphs: Charles grew up in a Monaco that belonged, in all but name, to Spain's sphere. His father Honoré I had spent nearly six decades as lord, sheltering under the 1524 deal with Charles V. By the time Charles took over in October 1581, he was in his mid-twenties and the arrangement was simply how things were.

Spain promised to protect the Rock. In return, Monaco did what Spain wanted. Charles kept his head down, and his short reign left little mark. He never married and had no children. When he died on 17 May 1589, the lordship passed to his younger brother Hercule.

claims.text: Charles II died unmarried and without children.
claims.note: All the family genealogies agree, which is why the lordship went to his brother.

claims.text: Under the 1524 treaties Spain was Monaco's protector, not its owner.
claims.note: The treaties of Burgos and Tordesillas recognised the lord's sovereignty, a point Monaco's historians stress.

reigns.hook: Charles leaves no son. His brother Hercule takes over, and Hercule is about to make himself the most hated man on the Rock.

reigns.tagline: The lord his own people threw into the sea
reigns.previously: Charles II dies unmarried. His brother Hercule is lord.
paragraphs: Hercule, Ercole to his Italian relatives, inherited Monaco from his brother in 1589. In 1595 he married Maria Landi, from a powerful family of northern Italian lords. Their son Honoré was born in 1597. On paper the future looked settled.

On the Rock, though, Hercule was hated. People accused him of preying on local women. On the night of 29 November 1604 a band of Monégasques ambushed and killed him. The story goes that they threw his body into the sea. His son Honoré was six, and Maria's brother Federico Landi stepped in to run Monaco for the boy.

claims.text: Hercule was killed by men whose wives and daughters he had abused, and his body thrown into the sea.
claims.note: The murder is certain. The revenge motive and the body in the sea come from later accounts and are hard to pin down.

claims.text: His wife's brother, Federico Landi, became regent for the young Honoré II.
claims.note: Landi's regency and his pro-Spanish line are well recorded.

reigns.hook: Monaco's lord is dead in the sea and his heir is six. His uncle Federico Landi takes charge, and Spanish soldiers will soon be marching in.

reigns.tagline: The boy lord who made himself a prince
reigns.previously: Lord Hercule has been murdered by his own people. His son is six.
paragraphs: Honoré was six when his father was killed. His mother's brother, Federico Landi, Prince of Val di Taro, ran Monaco as regent and kept it firmly on Spain's side. Spanish troops moved into his fortress in 1605, and the boy was taken off to Milan. From 1612 he called himself Prince of Monaco, and every ruler since has kept the title.

Spanish protection felt a lot like occupation, so Honoré quietly turned to France. In 1641 he signed the Treaty of Péronne with Louis XIII. That November his men turned on the Spanish garrison and threw it out. Spain seized his lands in Italy, so in 1642 Louis made him Duke of Valentinois, with French estates to make up the loss.

Honoré spent the rest of his life turning a grim fortress into a palace and filling it with hundreds of paintings. His only son, Hercule, died in a shooting accident in 1651. So when Honoré died in 1662, Monaco went to his grandson Louis.

claims.text: The Spanish soldiers were got drunk before Honoré's men threw them out.
claims.note: A favourite Monaco story. The expulsion of 1641 is well recorded; the party before it is not.

claims.text: Honoré II was the first ruler of Monaco to call himself prince.
claims.note: He took the title in 1612, and his documents from then on use it.

claims.text: Louis XIII made him Duke of Valentinois in 1642.
claims.note: The letters creating the duchy survive, and the title is still held by Monaco's rulers.

reigns.hook: Monaco is France's friend now. Honoré's grandson Louis I would much rather be at Louis XIV's court than on the Rock.

reigns.tagline: The courtier prince who went broke in Rome
reigns.previously: Honoré II dies a French duke. His grandson Louis takes over.
paragraphs: Louis was nine when his father died in a shooting accident, so he inherited straight from his grandfather Honoré II in 1662. He was a man of Louis XIV's court. He had married Catherine-Charlotte de Gramont, a marshal's daughter, in 1660, and he rode to war in the Sun King's campaigns.

At home he gave Monaco a proper legal code, the Code Louis, in 1678. His marriage was less tidy. Catherine-Charlotte was the talk of the court, and her name was linked with the king himself. She died in 1678.

In 1699 Louis XIV sent him to Rome as ambassador to the pope, to work on the looming fight over the Spanish throne. Louis put on a dazzling show and ran up enormous debts doing it. He died in Rome on 3 January 1701, and his son Antoine became prince.

claims.text: Louis I's wife was Louis XIV's lover.
claims.note: Court gossip and memoirs of the 1660s say so. They hint strongly but prove nothing.

claims.text: Louis I ruined himself keeping up a grand style as ambassador in Rome.
claims.note: His lavish embassy and his debts are recorded, but the tale of financial ruin grew in the retelling.

claims.text: He issued Monaco's law code, the Code Louis, in 1678.
claims.note: The code is named after him and stayed in force for well over a century.

reigns.hook: Louis dies far from home, deep in debt. His son Antoine is a giant of a man who would rather conduct an orchestra than lead an army.

reigns.tagline: The music-loving giant with no son
reigns.previously: Louis I dies in Rome, deep in debt. His son Antoine is prince.
paragraphs: Antoine was born in Paris and grew up at Louis XIV's court. He was huge, and the court nicknamed him Goliath. He served in the king's wars, but his real passion was music. He played, collected scores and kept musicians around him. In 1688 he married Marie de Lorraine-Armagnac, from one of France's grandest families. It was not a happy match.

The bigger problem was that they had only daughters. To keep Monaco in the family, Antoine married his eldest, Louise-Hippolyte, to a Frenchman, Jacques de Goyon de Matignon, in 1715. The deal was that Jacques would take the Grimaldi name and arms. When Antoine died on 20 February 1731, Louise-Hippolyte became Princess of Monaco.

claims.text: Antoine was so big that he was nicknamed Goliath.
claims.note: The nickname turns up in many popular histories; it is hard to trace to a source from his lifetime.

claims.text: Jacques de Matignon had to take the Grimaldi name and arms to marry Louise-Hippolyte.
claims.note: It was a condition of the 1715 marriage contract, meant to keep Monaco a Grimaldi state.

reigns.hook: For the first and only time, a woman reigns as Princess of Monaco. Louise-Hippolyte hurries home to the Rock to claim it.

reigns.tagline: Monaco's only reigning princess, gone in ten months
reigns.cameToPower: Inherited, as her father had no son
reigns.previously: Antoine I dies with no son. His daughter inherits Monaco.
paragraphs: Louise-Hippolyte was born in the palace at Monaco in 1697. Married off at 17 to a French nobleman, she had spent years in France raising a large family. When her father died in February 1731, she came home to take charge.

Monaco welcomed her warmly. Her husband Jacques, a Frenchman, was another matter. Then smallpox broke out. She caught it and died on 29 December 1731, just ten months into her reign. She was 34. The throne passed to the husband nobody wanted.

claims.text: Louise-Hippolyte is the only woman to have reigned as Princess of Monaco in her own right.
claims.note: Every list of Monaco's rulers agrees. Claudine, in the 1450s, was a lady, not a princess.

claims.text: She died of smallpox in Monaco in December 1731.
claims.note: Her death and its cause are recorded in the palace archives used by Saige and Labande.

reigns.hook: The princess is dead after ten months. Her French husband Jacques now claims the throne, and Monaco has made it clear it does not want him.

reigns.tagline: The Frenchman Monaco never wanted
reigns.previously: Louise-Hippolyte dies of smallpox, ten months into her reign.
paragraphs: Jacques was born a Goyon de Matignon in Normandy and became a Grimaldi only by marriage. When his wife died, he took the throne as Jacques I. Monaco's people saw him as a French outsider and never accepted him.

He did not try very hard. In May 1732 he left for Paris and handed day-to-day rule to Antoine, the Chevalier de Grimaldi, Antoine I's son born outside marriage. In November 1733 Jacques abdicated in favour of his son Honoré, then 12. He lived on in Paris until 1751. His mansion there, the Hôtel Matignon, is now the French prime minister's home.

claims.text: The Hôtel Matignon in Paris takes its name from Jacques's family.
claims.note: He bought the house in the 1720s; it has been the French prime minister's residence since 1935.

claims.text: Monaco refused to accept Jacques as its prince.
claims.note: His unpopularity is widely reported, but how far it drove him out, rather than his own preference for Paris, is unclear.

reigns.hook: Jacques goes back to Paris for good. The new prince is his 12-year-old son Honoré, who will also prefer Paris to the Rock.

reigns.tagline: The absent prince the Revolution swept away
reigns.previously: Jacques I gives up the throne and hands it to his young son Honoré.
paragraphs: Honoré became prince at twelve and left the ruling to his uncle Antoine, known as the Chevalier de Grimaldi, who governed Monaco for decades. Honoré preferred France. He soldiered for Louis XV and fought at Fontenoy in 1745, then settled into the good life in Paris.

In 1757 he married Maria Caterina Brignole, a rich Genoese heiress. It went badly. She left him, and after Honoré's death she married the Prince of Condé, one of the grandest nobles in France. Their son, the future Honoré IV, married Louise d'Aumont, heiress to the Mazarin fortune, tying the family ever tighter to France.

Then came the Revolution. Its ideas reached the Rock, and in January 1793 Monaco's people deposed their absent prince. Honoré was arrested in Paris and locked up. He came out alive but ruined, and died in Paris in March 1795.

claims.text: Honoré III fought at the Battle of Fontenoy in 1745.
claims.note: His service in the French army is recorded in the standard histories of Monaco.

claims.text: His estranged wife went on to marry the Prince of Condé.
claims.note: They married in exile after Honoré's death; the long affair before it was public knowledge.

reigns.hook: The prince is gone. Monaco is about to vote itself out of existence and become part of France.

reigns.title: Monaco Becomes French
reigns.tagline: No prince, no palace, no Monaco
reigns.previously: Revolution reaches the Rock. Monaco deposes Honoré III.
paragraphs: With Honoré III gone, Monaco's revolutionaries set up their own National Convention. In February 1793 France annexed the place outright. Monaco was renamed Fort d'Hercule, after the old legend that Hercules had passed this way. The Grimaldis had lost everything.

The palace was stripped. Its furniture and the princes' great art collection were sold off, and the building became a hospital and a poorhouse. The family suffered too. Françoise-Thérèse de Choiseul-Stainville, married to Honoré III's younger son Joseph, was guillotined in Paris on 27 July 1794. That same day Robespierre fell from power.
Monaco rode along through Napoleon's empire as a small French town. When Napoleon fell, the peace of 1814 gave Monaco back to the Grimaldis.

claims.text: Monaco was renamed Fort d'Hercule.
claims.note: The name appears in the French records of the annexation.

claims.text: One more day would have saved Françoise-Thérèse.
claims.note: She died on the day Robespierre fell, and the killing slowed soon after. Whether she would have been spared is guesswork.

reigns.hook: Napoleon is on Elba, and Honoré III's son Honoré IV is prince again. But he is sick, and Napoleon won't stay on Elba for long.

reigns.tagline: The sick prince who got his country back
reigns.cameToPower: Restored by the 1814 Treaty of Paris
reigns.previously: Napoleon has fallen, and the peace of 1814 hands Monaco back.
paragraphs: Honoré IV had been prince in name only since his father died in 1795. During the Terror he was thrown in prison. His wife, the rich heiress Louise d'Aumont, left him and divorced him under the new revolutionary laws. He came out of the Revolution poor and in poor health.

Then Napoleon fell, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 May 1814 gave Monaco back to the Grimaldis. Honoré was too ill to rule. His brother Joseph took charge at first, then his son, the future Honoré V, ran things from 1815. That year the peace settlement swapped French protection for that of the Kingdom of Sardinia. Honoré died in Paris in February 1819.

claims.text: The Treaty of Paris of 30 May 1814 restored Monaco to the Grimaldis.
claims.note: The treaty names the prince of Monaco among those whose rights were restored.

claims.text: His wife Louise d'Aumont divorced him during the Revolution.
claims.note: The divorce is recorded; she took back the Mazarin fortune she had brought to the marriage.

reigns.hook: Honoré IV is prince again, but too sick to rule. His son Honoré sets off for Monaco and meets Napoleon on the road.

reigns.tagline: The prince who met Napoleon on the road home
reigns.previously: Honoré IV dies in Paris. His son has run Monaco for years already.
paragraphs: Honoré had served Napoleon, as a soldier and at the Empress Joséphine's court. In March 1815 he was on his way to take charge of Monaco for his ailing father when he ran into Napoleon himself, just landed from Elba, near Cannes. Both men were heading home to take back a throne. Only one of them kept his.

Honoré became prince in 1819 and treated Monaco like a business that had to pay. He set up state monopolies, on flour and bread among other things, and squeezed taxes out of his subjects. The people of Menton and Roquebrune hated it, and he spent much of his time in Paris anyway. He never married. He died in Paris in 1841, and his brother Florestan inherited.

claims.text: Napoleon asked Honoré where he was going. Told “home to Monaco”, he replied that he was going home too, to the Tuileries.
claims.note: The meeting is told in many histories. The neat exchange has surely been polished in the retelling.

claims.text: Honoré V ran Monaco through state monopolies and heavy taxes.
claims.note: His monopoly system is described in all the standard histories and fed the 1848 revolt.

reigns.hook: Honoré V dies with no wife and no legitimate son. Monaco goes to his brother Florestan, a man who once trod the boards of the Paris stage.

reigns.tagline: The actor prince who lost most of Monaco
reigns.previously: Honoré V dies unmarried. His brother Florestan becomes prince.
paragraphs: Nobody expected Florestan to rule. He was a younger son with no prospects, and he spent time on the Paris stage. In 1816 he married Caroline Gibert, a clever, practical woman, and when he became prince at 55 she did much of the ruling.

They inherited a country seething over Honoré V's taxes. In 1848, the year revolutions swept Europe, Menton and Roquebrune rose up and declared themselves free towns under Sardinian protection. Monaco was left with the Rock and a strip of shore. Florestan died in Paris in June 1856, and his son Charles took over what was left.

claims.text: Florestan worked as an actor in Paris before he inherited.
claims.note: It appears in most histories of the family, but how serious a stage career it was is unclear.

claims.text: Menton and Roquebrune declared themselves free towns in 1848.
claims.note: They broke away during the 1848 revolutions and never came back to Monaco.

claims.text: Princess Caroline was the real ruler during Florestan's reign.
claims.note: Her strong hand is widely reported, but family histories may overstate it.

reigns.hook: Monaco has lost most of its land and most of its income. Florestan's son Charles needs a new idea, fast.

reigns.tagline: The prince who bet his country on a casino
reigns.previously: Florestan dies. Monaco has shrunk to the Rock and a strip of shore.
paragraphs: Charles III inherited a country that had almost vanished. In 1861 he made the loss official. France paid 4 million francs, Monaco gave up its claim to Menton and Roquebrune, and France recognised Monaco as independent. What Charles had left was a rock, a harbour, a bare hillside and plenty of sunshine.

So he bet on gambling. The first casinos struggled until 1863, when the businessman François Blanc took over the casino company, the Société des Bains de Mer. Blanc built big and advertised hard. In 1866 the plateau of Les Spélugues was renamed Monte Carlo, Charles's Mount, in the prince's honour. When the railway arrived in 1868, the crowds followed.

The money poured in. In 1869 Charles scrapped direct taxes on Monaco's residents, which helped make the place what it still is. He went blind in later life. He died in 1889, and his son Albert became prince.

claims.text: France paid Monaco 4 million francs under the 1861 treaty.
claims.note: The sum is written into the treaty.

claims.text: Monaco abolished direct taxes on its residents in 1869.
claims.note: A princely decree; casino money made it possible.

claims.text: “Sometimes red wins, sometimes black, but Blanc always wins.”
claims.note: A gamblers' joke from the 19th century. Nobody knows who first said it.

reigns.hook: Charles's son Albert has spent half his life at sea. Monaco's next prince is happier on a ship's deck than in a palace.

reigns.tagline: The prince who'd rather be at sea
reigns.previously: Charles III dies blind but rich, thanks to the casino.
paragraphs: Albert served in the Spanish navy as a young man, and the sea never let him go. He spent years on scientific cruises aboard his yachts, the Hirondelle and the Princesse Alice, hauling up deep-sea creatures and studying currents. He founded the Oceanographic Museum in Monaco, opened in 1910, and the Oceanographic Institute in Paris. He also set up the Institute of Human Paleontology in Paris.

His private life was rockier. His first marriage, to the Scottish noblewoman Lady Mary Victoria Hamilton, gave him a son, Louis, and was then annulled. His second wife, the American-born Alice Heine, was a great patron of the arts, but they separated. Albert also stood up for Alfred Dreyfus when that was far from popular.

At home, people wanted a say. After protests, Albert granted Monaco its first constitution in 1911. The same year the first Monte Carlo Rally set off. He died in Paris in 1922, and his son Louis became prince.

claims.text: Albert I openly supported Alfred Dreyfus.
claims.note: His backing for a retrial is documented in his letters and in histories of the Dreyfus affair.

claims.text: The Oceanographic Museum opened in 1910.
claims.note: The museum's opening is well documented; it still stands on the cliff of the Rock.

reigns.hook: Louis II is a soldier with no wife and no legitimate child. If he dies without an heir, Monaco could pass to a German duke.

reigns.tagline: The old soldier who saved the throne by adoption
reigns.previously: Albert the Navigator dies in Paris. His son Louis is the new prince.
paragraphs: Louis spent his life in the French army and was a general in the First World War. He never married, but he had a daughter, Charlotte, born in Algeria in 1898 to Marie Juliette Louvet, a cabaret singer. That turned out to matter a great deal.

A 1918 treaty with France said that if the Grimaldi line died out, Monaco would come under France. Next in line by blood stood a German cousin, the Duke of Urach, and France would never accept him. The fix: in 1919 Louis adopted Charlotte and made her his heir.

In the Second World War Monaco was occupied, first by Italy, then by Germany. In 1944 Charlotte gave up her rights in favour of her son Rainier. Louis finally married in 1946, to the actress Ghislaine Dommanget, and died in 1949. Monaco's football stadium, the Stade Louis II, carries his name.

claims.text: Louis adopted his daughter Charlotte in 1919 to keep the throne from a German cousin.
claims.note: The adoption and the succession worry behind it are fully documented.

claims.text: The 1918 treaty tied Monaco's fate to France if the Grimaldis died out.
claims.note: The treaty text is public; a 2002 treaty later changed the rule.

reigns.hook: Louis's grandson Rainier is 25 and in charge. He has big plans for Monaco, and soon a famous bride.

reigns.tagline: The prince who married a film star and built a city
reigns.previously: Louis II dies at 78. His grandson Rainier takes the throne.
paragraphs: Rainier became prince at 25. In April 1956 he married the Hollywood star Grace Kelly, and the wedding put Monaco in newspapers around the world. They had three children: Caroline in 1957, Albert in 1958 and Stéphanie in 1965. After years of fighting over the casino company, Rainier had the state flood it with new shares in 1966, and the tycoon Aristotle Onassis sold up.

In 1962 he gave Monaco a new constitution. The same year he picked a fight he couldn't win. Charles de Gaulle, angry that French people were dodging tax in Monaco, set up customs checks on the border. Under the deal that ended the row in 1963, French residents in Monaco pay French tax.

Rainier pushed the coastline out, building the Fontvieille district on land reclaimed from the sea, and let tower blocks rise. Hence the Builder Prince. On 14 September 1982 Grace died after a car crash. Rainier never remarried. He died on 6 April 2005, after a reign of almost 56 years.

claims.text: Grace Kelly died after a car crash on 14 September 1982.
claims.note: Her doctors said she had a mild stroke at the wheel the day before. Stéphanie was in the car and survived.

claims.text: Rainier squeezed Onassis out of the casino company in 1966–67.
claims.note: In 1966 the state created 600,000 new shares for itself; Onassis lost a court challenge and sold out in 1967.

claims.text: Since 1963, French people living in Monaco pay French tax.
claims.note: Set by the 1963 Franco-Monegasque tax convention.

reigns.hook: Rainier is dead. His only son, Albert, a former Olympic bobsledder, takes the throne at 47.

reigns.tagline: The Olympian prince with a green cause
reigns.previously: Rainier dies after nearly 56 years. His son Albert takes over.
paragraphs: Albert was born in the palace in 1958 and studied political science at Amherst College in the United States. He was a serious athlete. He competed in bobsleigh at five Winter Olympics, from Calgary in 1988 to Salt Lake City in 2002, and he has sat on the International Olympic Committee since 1985. He became regent in March 2005 as his father lay dying, and prince when Rainier died that April.

He has made the environment his cause, above all the oceans and the climate. In April 2006 he reached the North Pole, and that year he set up the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation to fund environmental work. In July 2011 he married Charlene Wittstock, a South African Olympic swimmer.

On 10 December 2014 Charlene gave birth to twins, Gabriella and Jacques. Jacques is heir to the throne. Before his marriage Albert had two other children, both of whom he has publicly acknowledged. More than seven centuries after a fake friar slipped through the gate, a Grimaldi still rules the Rock.

claims.text: Albert competed in bobsleigh at five Winter Olympics.
claims.note: Olympic records list him at every Winter Games from 1988 to 2002.

claims.text: He reached the North Pole in April 2006.
claims.note: The expedition was announced by the palace and widely reported.

claims.text: Jacques, born on 10 December 2014, is heir to the throne.
claims.note: Monaco's succession rules put sons before daughters, so he comes ahead of his twin sister.
